transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date: 2026-03-01
- Time: 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~70 minutes
- Recording id: ff-20260301-7b3c9f
- Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Ruth Nguyen (Redwood SE), Priya Rao (Velox ML Lead), Samir Patel (Velox Infra), Lena Cho (Velox CTO), Noah Green (Velox SRE)

Summary:
Redwood and Velox ran a deep technical workshop focused on concrete perf tradeoffs for Llama/Mistral/Qwen families and MoE routing costs when operating in an on-prem (VPC-like) environment. Primary goals were: clarify rope scaling impacts for long contexts, quantify MoE routing overhead and token duplication, validate KV/prefix cache strategies and batching configs, and agree on an on-prem benchmark plan. We surfaced network egress and intra-node comms costs for dedicated routing, discussed quantization (q4/q8) artifacts and kernel selection, and left with concrete test tasks and access items.

Topics covered:
- MoE routing overhead and cost model (per-token routing, experts hot-spotting)
- Rope scaling mismatches when moving from 2k->32k contexts, and impact on attention kernels
- KV cache/prefix caching patterns to reduce duplicate computation for high-reuse sessions
- Batching and sequence-length-aware batching policies for mixed workloads
- Quantization tradeoffs (q4 vs q8, outlier handling, activation quant noise)
- On-prem/HW considerations: H100 vs A100, NVLink/PCIe topology, NCCL ring implications
- Network and VPC constraints: RPC fanout, control-plane vs data-plane routing, egress costs
- Practical benchmark plan for Velox private deployment

Action items recap:
- Redwood to run benchmark on Velox cluster with the two model families (qwen-15b, mistral-7b) and one MoE variant; measure throughput, 95/99/99.9p latencies, and token cost delta between hosted and on-prem profiles.
- Velox to provide traces and hardware access windows.
- Share docs: quantization bench sheet, KV cache design note, routing-cost calculator spreadsheet.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): Alright, thanks everyone for taking the slot. I'm gonna hand to Diego to kick off with the high-level goals, and then we'll get into numbers.
[00:22] Diego (SE): Cool thanks. So, Velox said they see a fairly mixy ahm - mixed seq length distribution, a lotta short requests but a fat tail of long context stateful sessions up to 10k tokens. The ask here is: how do we keep 99p latency acceptable without paying 3x token cost. We're going to talk MoE routing, rope scaling, and caching.
[00:45] Priya (Velox): Yep that's correct. We also mess with long form summarization pipelines so long contexts matter.
[01:10] Ruth (SE): Quick intro — for MoE costs the obvious part is extra flops from duplicated tokens when you route to multiple experts and dynamic routing overhead — but there's also scheduling overhead inside the runtime and memory pressure from per-expert caches.
[01:34] Samir (Velox): When you say duplicated tokens, is that the same thing as token fanout? Can you define it simply?
[01:42] Diego (SE): Yeah, token fanout is the number of experts a token is dispatched to. If gating sends to top-2 experts, you potentially double compute per token plus memory shuffles. In practice the router sparsity and load-balance matters — a pathological layer can hot-spot and create 4-5x effective work.
[02:07] Priya: And routing also causes more KV cache fragmentation? we've seen kv cache misses increase when switching to MoE.
[02:16] Diego: Exactly. If two tokens for the same conversation get routed to different experts at different layers, your cached key/value layout can't be reused as effectively. That's where token affinity caching and sticky routing heuristics help.
[02:35] Lena (CTO): Sticky routing meaning we force tokens from same conversation to prefer same expert set? Isn't that going to worsen balance?
[02:42] Ruth: There's a tradeoff. You can use affinity windows — for a conversation session we maintain a small affinity table, prefer the previously used expert ordering unless load imbalance exceeds threshold. That reduces KV churn but you might need periodic rebalancing.
[03:05] Noah (SRE): Could that rebalancing trigger big NCCL spikes on the network? We can't have huge ring storms on our H100 mesh.
[03:14] Diego: Yes, rebalancing and expert reshuffles cause network shuffle. We recommend doing rebalances during tail-scheduled low-load times or staggered windowed checkpoints. Also topology-aware kernels reduce cross-node transfers.
[03:30] Priya: Let's talk rope scaling. We bumped context beyond the model's original rope frequency and saw weird perf/accuracy drops.
[03:37] Diego: Sure. Two things — first, rotary positional encoding (rope) that was calibrated for a 2k max context may underrepresent phase at 16k/32k, causing degenerative attention weights. Second, many kernels assume fixed sequence length and the compilation chooses kernels optimized for that range. When you jump to 16k, different attention algorithm (chunked, flash attention variants) and different memory layout is needed.
[04:05] Ruth: To address the first, options are: 1) linear scaling of rope frequencies (rescale token frequency), 2) use ALiBi or other extrapolatable pos encodings, or 3) fine-tune a small adapter on long-context tokens to reduce drift. Each has latency/cost implications.
[04:25] Priya: Fine-tune might be good but we prefer not to touch proprietary weights. Can we do kernel-level changes without fine-tune?
[04:33] Diego: Yes, using modified attention kernels and careful compilation to use chunked attention for long sequences helps. But the model numerics can still degrade if the positional mechanism is mismatched. We'll show bench numbers.
[04:50] Maya: Quick pause — Ruth you had a chart on q4 vs q8 perf/accuracy; can you summarize the tradeoffs?
[04:57] Ruth: Sure. Q4 gives best memory and compute savings but is sensitive to outlier activations — you need per-channel outlier handling or an outlier-adapter (store a small FP16 residual) otherwise you lose 1-3 percent quality on perplexity or instruction-following for some models. Q8 (symmetric) keeps more fidelity, less speedup. For qwen we saw q4-maybe works but needs kludge for attention outliers.
[05:25] Priya: Are there model-specific kernels? Like Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen — do we need different compile paths?
[05:32] Diego: Yes. Qwen has wider hidden dims and requires different matmul tiling; Mistral's block-sparse FFN variants behave differently at low batch sizes. Llama family tends to be more predictable. Our runtime selects kernels per model-arch and observed seq-length distribution.
[05:55] Samir: On the on-prem side, our cluster is mixed H100 and A100, interconnect NVLink within nodes and Mellanox between nodes. Will that affect routing choices?
[06:06] Diego: Absolutely. H100 has better TensorCore perf for low-precision ops and different memory bandwidth. Also NCCL collective shapes differ — for MoE if experts are spread across GPUs, inter-node traffic increases. For Velox we'd recommend packing experts to reduce cross-node shuffles or using dedicated local-expert placement with fast sharding.
[06:30] Maya: We should call out the egress and RPC costs for private deployments. Even internal RPCs between racks can add latency; if you do a lot of routing across nodes you'll see 5-20ms penalties per hop depending on your fabric.
[06:45] Lena: That could break our 99p. Any mitigations that don't impact model accuracy?
[06:50] Ruth: Caching is the obvious one. Prefix/KV caching reduces the number of tokens that actually hit the full model. For example, repeated system prompts or conversation history can be cached at routing checkpoints and skip recomputation. For stateful sessions you can also store latent states per-session and only run delta tokens.
[07:10] Priya: Our workload is 70% short queries and 30% long sessions — wonder what batching policy is optimal.
[07:16] Diego: Sequence-length aware batching. Don't batch long sessions with many short queries— that drags latency. Maintain separate queues: a fast-path queue with small batch-size and pre-warmed KV cache and a long-path queue with chunked attention and larger batch.
[07:36] Samir: How aggressive do we go on batching to save cost without blowing p99?
[07:42] Ruth: We usually cap fast-path batch at 8-16 tokens, aim for <50ms tail for short queries. For long-path, batching gives throughput improvement but you'll need to accept higher p99 for those requests; the SLA can route those to dedicated capacity if you need lower latency.
[07:59] Maya: Let's ground this with numbers — Diego, you had a toy calc for MoE routing overhead for top-2 gating?
[08:06] Diego: Yup. Simple model: base model single-expert cost X tokens. With top-2 gating you pay roughly ~1.8X if experts are balanced (not exactly 2X because gating + sparsity). But if imbalance or hot-spot layer occurs it can spike to 3-4X. Network overhead can add a fixed 0.5-2ms per token depending on node boundaries.
[08:29] Priya: So worst-case our token costs could triple. But average might be +80%?
[08:33] Diego: That's a fair working estimate. We need bench runs to get real numbers on your cluster.
[08:42] Noah: For benchmark, we want: model, quantization profile, sequence length distribution, and routing sparsity configs. We'll schedule rubrics and measure 95/99/99.9.
[08:53] Maya: Great — runbook will be in the shared sheet. We'll need SSH access or a runner container.
[09:02] Samir: You mentioned prefix caching — what's the size of the KV store we should expect per session?
[09:09] Ruth: It depends on hidden dim and sequence length. Roughly speaking, KV size is O(seq_len * hidden_dim). For a 32k sequence on a 16k hidden state that’s ~ (32k * 16k * 2 bytes?) — rough math, could be multiple GBs if you store full FP16. Quantizing KV to int8 or 4-bit helps shrink memory by 2-4x but with retrieval noise.
[09:36] Priya: I'm worried about quantized KV noise causing hallucinations. Any strategies?
[09:41] Diego: Two things: 1) use hybrid KV: store recent keys in FP16 and cold keys quantized, 2) use a small residual FP16 correction for high-salience tokens. Both reduce memory while keeping correctness.
[09:56] Lena: What about the control-plane — SSO, audit logs — I know this is perf talk but Velox needs SAML, KMS integration for Private. Any perf implication?
[10:05] Maya: Generally minimal; auth occurs at request ingress. The bigger risk is if you route calls through a central control plane for model selection on every request — that adds RTT. We recommend local decisioning with a cached policy.
[10:20] Priya: Could you summarize best immediate mitigations: we have mixed H100/A100, long-tail sessions, and want to keep p99 under 200ms for short queries and <1s for long sessions where possible.
[10:31] Ruth: Short summary: 1) Use separate fast/long queues, 2) implement prefix/KV caching with affinity windows, 3) limit MoE fanout (top-1 or top-2 but with affinity), 4) prefer q8 for model-critical endpoints and q4 for background/batched throughput where small quality drop is acceptable, 5) do topology-aware expert placement and pack experts to minimize cross-node shuffles, 6) test rope scaling using adapter fine-tune if you can't change pos encodings.
[11:02] Diego: Also schedule rebalances during low-traffic windows and instrument per-layer routing histograms to detect hot-spots.
[11:10] Samir: OK can you walk quickly through the benchmark plan items so I capture them?
[11:14] Maya: Sure. We'll run three model configs: qwen-15b (q4/q8), mistral-7b (q4/q8), and a test MoE 12-expert toy model. For each: run short-query perf mix, long-session mix (synthetic traces), and extreme 32k context run. Collect throughput, 95/99/99.9 latencies, KV hit rates, router top-k distribution, NCCL counters.
[11:40] Priya: We'll provide the real traces. Also note we have some PII-ish prompts — MFA/PII gating — so we may need to anonymize.
[11:48] Maya: Totally fine, hashed traces are ok.
[11:52] Ruth: One more note on kernel selection: if you run with multi-precision paths (FP16 + int8 matmul) you may get different perf curves on H100 vs A100. We'll auto-detect but we'll send the kernel-selection heuristics so you can pin if needed.
[12:10] Diego: For MoE routing, we'll instrument and share a small router simulator that lets you tune top-k, capacity factor, and glue it to your trace to get estimated work multipliers before any large runs.
[12:23] Priya: That would be great, so we can preview costs.
[12:28] Maya: Okay recap — next steps and owners were listed. Anything else from Velox?
[12:33] Lena: Just timing — can you get the initial bench results by next week? We want to present to the infra board on the 12th.
[12:40] Maya: We'll aim for that.
[12:43] Samir: Quick question, on quantization: if we do q4 for the KV store only and keep the model weights q8, any quick wins?
[12:51] Ruth: That hybrid approach often gives the sweet spot — reduces memory pressure for KV while keeping matmul fidelity. You still need to handle outlier channels for the activations.
[13:05] Priya: And for rope scaling, can you share the small adapter approach? We don't want to full-fine-tune.
[13:11] Diego: Yes — small local fine-tune on a lightweight prefix adapter to adjust positional interpolation. It's quick and few-shot; we have a one-page recipe.
[13:20] Maya: We'll attach all referenced artifacts into the follow-up email: kernel heuristics, quant bench sheet, router sim link, and runbook.
[13:27] Noah: For the access window we can do Thurs 02:00–06:00 UTC. Does that work?
[13:32] Maya: Works for us. Diego, Ruth, want to take that?
[13:35] Diego: Yep we'll schedule.
[13:37] Ruth: I'll prepare the run harness container.
[13:40] Priya: Thanks team, this was super helpful.
[13:43] Maya: Thanks all — we'll send notes and schedule.
[13:47] [end recording]
